en: Theravāda Vinaya Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
The Chapter on the Naked (Naggavagga), Chapter 22: The Training Rule on the Bathing Cloth.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the Blessed One had authorized bathing robes for the bhikkhunīs.
The group of six bhikkhunīs,
thinking, "The Blessed One has authorized bathing robes," wore bathing robes of excessive dimensions.
They wander about dragging [the robes] both from the front and from behind.
Those bhikkhunīs who have few desires... [as before]... were indignant, complained, and grumbled, saying:
"How can the bhikkhunīs of the group of six wear water-sprinkling robes of unlimited size?"... [as before]...
“Is it true, monks, that the bhikkhunīs of the group of six are wearing water-sprinkling robes of unlimited size?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them... [as before]...
"How indeed, monks, can the group of six bhikkhunīs wear water-sprinkling robes of unlimited size?
This, monks, is neither for the inspiration of those without faith nor for the increase of the faith of those who have it...
And thus, monks, should the bhikkhunīs recite this training rule: "‘If a bhikkhunī wears a water-sprinkling robe that is of unlimited size, she commits an offense of wrong-doing.’"
“Now, when a nun is having a bathing-cloth made, it must be made according to the proper measure. Herein, this is the measure:
four spans long by the Sugata-span, and two spans wide. For one who exceeds that, there is an offense entailing cutting down and confession.
A bathing-cloth (udakasāṭikā) means:
She wears it while bathing.
"Having it made" means either making it herself or having it made by another. It should be made according to the prescribed measure.
In this regard, the measurement is as follows: four spans of the Sugata-span in length, and two spans across.
If one makes it or causes it to be made exceeding that, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the effort.
Upon obtaining it, having cut it down, a confession of an offense entailing expiation (*pācittiya*) must be made.
If one finishes what was begun by oneself, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one has others finish what was begun by oneself, there is an offense of expiation.
If one finishes by oneself what was begun by others, there is an offense of expiation.
If she has it finished by others after they have already begun it, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If she makes it herself or has it made for the sake of another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If she uses what has been made by another and obtained [by her], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense if one makes it the proper measure,
or makes it less than that.
If, having obtained something made by another that exceeds the proper measure, she cuts it down and uses it—
whether making a canopy, a floor-covering, a screen-wall, a mattress, or a pillow— for one who is insane;
"For one who is a first-offender.
The second training rule is concluded.
